# Circuits, voltage, current and resistance (Ohm's law) (`ohms_law_circuits`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electric_battery; helped by electromagnetism, symbolic_algebra
- Core idea: Current flows only round a closed loop of conductor. Three quantities must be kept apart: the push of the source (voltage), the flow (current) and the hindrance of the wire (resistance); current equals voltage divided by resistance. Resistance grows in proportion to the length of a wire and falls in proportion to its cross-section, and copper conducts about six times better than iron. Cells in series add their voltages; resistances in series add; in parallel branches the current divides. The power dissipated as heat is current squared times resistance. Multiply by elapsed time to find the energy delivered at steady current. A coil round a compass needle (galvanometer) measures current by the angle of deflection.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking that current is used up on its way round the circuit; the same current returns to the source, what is spent is energy
  - Using one word for voltage, current and power, as everyday speech does
  - Forgetting the internal resistance of the battery, which limits the current however thick the wire
  - Believing that it is the voltage alone that kills or heats; what matters is the current that the voltage can drive through the body or wire
- History: europe: 1781 – Cavendish finds the proportionality but does not publish; 1827 Ohm, Die galvanische Kette (rejected in Germany at first, honoured by the Royal Society in 1841); 1841 Joule, heating law; 1845 Kirchhoff, circuit laws
- Read:
  - Georg Simon Ohm, Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet (1827)
  - Bruce J. Hunt, Pursuing Power and Light: Technology and Physics from James Watt to Albert Einstein (2010)
